brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to CTFS - For TechIQ Attendees

questions.question: How many clinical trial financial modules make up the CTFS platform?
choices: Three modules
Five modules
Seven modules
Two modules
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—GrantPlan, Contracting, Forecasting, Site Payments, and Analytics make up the five-module suite.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course specifically outlines five modules that work together as one financial backbone. Review slide 10 to see each module and what it does.

questions.question: What is the primary problem that CTFS Contracting solves in the trial start-up process?
choices: Slowing down site recruitment timelines
Manual, error-prone contract execution that delays site activation and payments
Reducing the number of geographies CTFS can support
Eliminating the need for GrantPlan budgeting
questions.feedback_correct: You've identified the core problem—CTA processing is manual and fragile, and delays in contract signing ripple into delayed site activation and compressed timelines.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Contracting module addresses the manual, error-prone nature of contract execution and how delays in signing cascade into operational problems downstream. Slide 16 explains this problem clearly.

questions.question: Which discovery question would you ask a Clinical Operations Director like Gilbert to open a real conversation?
choices: What keeps you up at night from a compliance risk standpoint?
How are payment delays affecting your site relationships right now?
Where are your current AI investments stalling before they reach value?
How integrated are your current financial systems with your CRM?
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—this is the discovery question designed specifically for Gilbert, focusing on his operational pain around payment delays and site satisfaction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each persona has a different discovery question tailored to their specific concerns. Gilbert's world is trial execution and site satisfaction, so the discovery question should address payment cycle times and site relationships.

questions.question: What does it mean that CTFS Contracting is 'not a standalone tool'?
choices: It cannot be used by sponsors running fewer than 50 trials per year
Signed CTAs automatically inform payment milestones and update budget alignment without manual re-entry
It requires a separate licensing agreement from the other CTFS modules
It only works for digital-native pharmaceutical companies
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the distinction is that Contracting is upstream in the unified financial lifecycle and automatically triggers downstream processes in Site Payments and GrantPlan.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The value of Contracting lies in its integration with the rest of the CTFS suite. When a contract is signed, it doesn't sit in isolation—it automatically informs payment milestones and budget updates. This unification is what separates CTFS from point solutions.

questions.question: You are talking to Reena, the VP IT Clinical, and she asks 'How do I modernize without breaking compliance or creating new integration nightmares?' What does this tell you about her core concern?
choices: She is worried that the solution will be too expensive for her budget
She is primarily focused on speed of implementation and quick wins
She needs to trust the architecture and governance before she trusts the pitch
She is uncertain whether CTFS can handle the geographic complexity of global trials
questions.feedback_correct: You've correctly identified what Reena is really asking—her concern is about architectural integrity, compliance risk, and avoiding new integration problems. Trust in the system design comes first for her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Understanding what each persona is really asking beneath the surface is crucial for a strong response. Reena's question reveals that she prioritizes governance and technical architecture over speed. Her objections will likely center on integration risk and audit readiness.

questions.question: A buyer tells you 'We already have a system.' According to the course, what should your first move be?
choices: Immediately list the competitive features of CTFS that their system doesn't have
Ask what it does not unify and quantify the cost of that gap
Suggest a 30-day pilot to demonstrate CTFS superiority
Acknowledge their investment and pivot directly to the $15 billion proof point
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—asking about gaps in unification opens a real conversation, because the honest answer often reveals where manual processes and reconciliation costs still exist.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course explicitly warns against leading with feature comparison. Instead, the stronger move is to understand what their system doesn't unify and help them quantify the operational or financial cost of that fragmentation.

questions.question: A sponsor running 100+ trials per year is interested in Contracting but concerned about the timing since the module just launched. What is the strongest response to their timing concern?
choices: Early adopters will receive the module at a discounted rate for the first year
The rest of the CTFS suite is proven at scale and Contracting completes the upstream coverage; early adopters gain input into the product roadmap
Waiting longer will make adoption more expensive due to planned price increases
Late adopters will be required to go through extended training and validation periods
questions.feedback_correct: You've identified the core value argument—Contracting fills the last gap in a proven platform, and early movers gain strategic influence over product development.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The timing concern is real, but the answer is rooted in the unification story and the opportunity to shape the roadmap. Slide 20 explains that early adoption isn't a risk when the foundation is already proven at $15 billion in transaction volume.

questions.question: After a conversation at TechIQ with a sponsor's Clinical Operations Director, you observe three signals: expressed pain about payment delays, willingness to continue the conversation, and indication of budget visibility. How should you classify this lead?
choices: Not qualified—you need a commitment to a demo within 30 days before it counts
Partially qualified—you have expressed pain but need to establish a named decision-maker
Fully qualified—multiple strong signals are present, and at least one is sufficient to move forward
Overqualified—this contact has too much budget visibility to be a typical early-stage opportunity
questions.feedback_correct: You've correctly applied the qualification framework—one strong signal is enough, and this lead shows multiple signals (pain, willingness to continue, budget visibility), making it clearly qualified.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Qualification doesn't require all signals or a formal demo commitment at the conversation stage. The course teaches that expressed pain, a named decision-maker, openness to a demo, or budget visibility—even just one—is sufficient to qualify a lead for follow-up.

questions.question: You are building your 30-day follow-up plan for a contact from TechIQ who expressed concern about forecasting accuracy but seemed hesitant about timelines. What makes the follow-up action 'personalized' versus generic?
choices: Sending them the CTFS brochure rather than asking for a meeting immediately
Referencing the specific pain they raised (forecasting accuracy) and offering a targeted resource or demo that directly addresses it
Following up within 48 hours instead of waiting a week
Using their first name and mentioning the company they work for in the subject line
questions.feedback_correct: Personalization means the follow-up connects directly to what they said at TechIQ—in this case, their concern about forecasting—not just a generic check-in.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Generic follow-up email loses credibility and momentum. The course emphasizes that personalization means referencing the exact pain they raised and structuring the action (demo, resource, call) around that specific concern.

questions.question: Which of the following best represents the core competitive distinction of CTFS that you should lead with when speaking to any buyer at TechIQ?
choices: CTFS has more features than any competitor and processes more payments
CTFS unifies the entire financial lifecycle and eliminates data handoff friction that point solutions require
CTFS is the only platform that offers both Contracting and Forecasting modules
CTFS supports more geographies than GreenPhire and has faster contract processing than Medidata
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—the course explicitly states this is where CTFS wins, and it's the story you should lead with instead of feature-by-feature comparison.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course warns against leading with feature comparison or competitive positioning based on individual capabilities. The unification story—solving the whole financial lifecycle and eliminating the integration problems that point solutions create—is the strategic advantage.
